title: SRE Documentation Standards: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
body:
Overview

This document defines the canonical SRE documentation standards used at Redwood Inference for: SLOs and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and runbooks. The goal is to ensure consistent, actionable, and auditable operational artifacts across all services so teams can reliably operate and evolve the platform.

Scope

Applies to: all public and internal-facing services owned or operated by Redwood Inference (hosted API, control plane services, autoscaling controllers, inference runtime, and edge components). Exemptions require an explicit documented approval from the SRE manager.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

Purpose
- Define expected service behavior that reflects customer experience.
- Drive prioritization between feature work and reliability work through error budgets.

SLO definition requirements (every SLO doc must include):
- Service name and component(s) covered (e.g., api-frontend, kv-cache, model-router).
- Persona and user impact (end-user, internal, partner).
- Observable metric (one primary metric; e.g., request success rate, p99 latency, inference-token-completion time).
- SLO target (expressed as percentage or latency bound) and measurement window.
- SLI measurement method (prometheus/trace-based query, sampling rate, which labels are used).
- Owner (primary and secondary oncall/team).
- Enforcement policy and thresholds for alerts and automated actions.
- Link to dashboards and alert rules.

SLO examples
| Service | SLO (primary) | Measurement window | Alert threshold |
| api-frontend | 99.95% successful requests (4xx/5xx excluded) | 30d | 99.9% over 7d -> P1 alert |
| inference-runtime | p99 end-to-end token latency <= 1200ms | 14d | p99 > 1400ms for 1h -> P1 alert |
| embeddings-service | 99.9% request success | 30d | 99.7% over 7d -> P2 alert |

Error budget policy
- Error budget = 100% - SLO target (over the defined window). Teams must track burn-rate via the error-budget dashboard.
- Burn-rate actions (automated and human):
  - Burn-rate > 2x for 30m: alert P1 to oncall and pause non-critical rollouts.
  - Burn-rate > 5x for 15m: engage oncall + paging to engineering manager, execute mitigation runbook.
  - If error budget exhausted for the window: suspend feature rollouts and schedule reliability sprint within 3 working days.
- Rollout gating: all canary rollouts default to a 1% traffic canary, expanded only when burn-rate remains <=1.2x for the canary window.

Alerting and escalation
- Alerts must map to SLO thresholds and include: service, metric, current window value, error budget burn-rate, runbook link, and suggested immediate actions.
- Escalation path: oncall -> service owner -> engineering manager -> SRE lead (timings defined in runbook per P-level).

2) Capacity Planning

Principles
- Plan for predictable workload growth and transient load (batch jobs, model warmups, release events).
- Capacity targets align with business commitments (Dedicated capacity customers SLA, public API throughput targets).
- Use cost-aware safety margins: aim to meet peak demand at 95th percentile traffic with autoscale headroom for transient spikes.

Capacity doc requirements (per service):
- Current baseline throughput and utilization (1h, 24h, 7d, 30d charts).
- Peak historical day and projected growth rate (monthly and 12-month forecast).
- Scaling policy(s) and autoscaler settings (min/max replicas, CPU/GPU utilization targets, queue-depth thresholds).
- Headroom policy: recommended spare capacity (e.g., reserve 15% of GPU capacity for cross-zone failover).
- Runbook references for capacity incidents (throttling, OOM, disk pressure).

Capacity planning procedure (quarterly cadence):
1. Gather utilization and request-profile telemetry.
2. Forecast N, P95, and peak hourly demand for next quarter and next 12 months.
3. Translate demand to resource needs (GPU hours, instance counts, memory).
4. Validate against procurement / cloud commitments and recommend reserved capacity or burst strategies.
5. Publish capacity plan, owners, and mitigation strategies.

Capacity thresholds (example table)
| Resource | Healthy | Warning | Critical |
| GPU pool (inference-prod-us-west) | utilization <= 75% | 75-90% | >90% |
| API p99 latency | <= 800ms | 800-1200ms | >1200ms |
| Queue depth | < 50ms avg wait | 50-200ms avg wait | >200ms avg wait |

3) Reliability Initiatives and Investment

Types of initiatives
- Preventive: capacity right-sizing, load-shedding design, model quantization to reduce tail latency.
- Detective: improved SLIs/coverage, synthetic canaries, chaos testing.
- Corrective: refactors of hot paths, redispatch/pinning fixes, kernel updates in runtime.

Prioritization 
- Use a simple ROI rubric: impact on SLO, cost to implement, probability of recurrence, and scope of affected customers.
- Major initiatives must produce: a hypothesis, test plan (metrics and acceptance criteria), rollout plan, rollback plan, and close-the-loop verification (post-implementation SLI check for 14 days).

Milestones and tracking
- Maintain a Reliability Initiative board (quarterly goals). Each initiative should contain owners, start/end dates, success metrics, and a link to associated runbooks or PRs.

4) Incident Review and Postmortem Standards

Postmortem requirements (for any P1, and for P2s where learning is material):
- Title, incident timeline (with timestamps in UTC), detection and mitigation steps, root cause analysis, contributing factors, impact summary (customers affected, downtime, revenue/regulatory impact if known), and follow-up actions with owners and due dates.
- Postmortem tone: blameless, factual, and specific. Use the 5-Why technique and include supporting telemetry screenshots or links.
- Severity classification guidance and SLA for publishing: P1 postmortems published within 48 hours as draft, final within 7 days. P2 final within 14 days.

Incident review checklist
1. Did the alert fire as expected? Link to alert runbook.
2. Was the runbook adequate? If not, update with missing steps.
3. Was the oncall escalation followed?
4. Are there code or config changes required? Assign owners.
5. Schedule a post-incident review meeting and assign action items.

5) Operational Tooling and Observability

Required tooling and dashboards
- Metrics: Prometheus + Thanos for retention. Dashboards in Grafana organized by service, SLO, and critical subsystem (compute, network, datastore).
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry + Jaeger for end-to-end traces; ensure span sampling allows p99 detection for high-traffic endpoints.
- Logging: ELK stack with structured JSON logs; retention and indices per data management policy.
- Synthetic checks: synthetic inference canary that runs a small set of prompts every 60s across regions.
- Error-budget dashboard: per-SLO burn-rate panels, top contributing error reasons, and remaining budget.

Instrumentation expectations
- All production services must emit at least one success/failure metric and one latency histogram.
- Important labels: service, region, model-version, route, and customer-tier.

Operational automation
- Automated rollback: where possible, use traffic routing to fallback to a compatible model variant when SLO breach is detected.
- Canary gating automation: pipeline must halt rollout expansion if canary burn-rate > 1.2x.

6) SRE Runbook Template (required fields)

Every runbook must be explicitly linked from the SLO and the alert definition. Minimum content:
- Runbook title and short description.
- Pager steps (immediate actions to reduce customer impact).
- Quick checks (what to look for in dashboards/logs/traces).
- Mitigation steps (short-term) and remediation (long-term).
- Rollback / switch-over commands and safety notes.
- Post-incident actions and owner contact info.
- Last tested date and test run summary.

Runbook example (abbreviated)
1) Title: inference-runtime - elevated p99 latency
2) Pager steps:
   a) Check error-budget dashboard and current burn-rate.
   b) Identify top contributing models by trace tag model-version.
   c) If p99 > 1400ms and burn-rate > 2x: scale up inference pool by +25% (kubectl/scale CLI snippet below).

kubectl scale deploy inference-runtime --replicas=$(($(kubectl get deploy inference-runtime -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}')*125/100))

3) If scaling does not restore SLO within 5 minutes: route 20% of traffic to fallback model-quantized-v1 and notify owners.

7) Ownership and Review Cadence

- SLO owner: responsible for maintaining the SLO, dashboard, and runbooks. Must review SLOs quarterly.
- Capacity owner: responsible for quarterly capacity plan updates and procurement requests.
- Runbook owner: validate runbook steps every 90 days and record the last-tested date in the runbook.
- Postmortem owner: ensure actions are tracked to completion.

Governance and audits
- SRE leadership will perform an annual documentation audit to ensure every production service has: an SLO, an owner, an up-to-date runbook, and a capacity plan.

Appendix A: Common SLIs and queries (examples)
- Successful requests SLI (Prometheus): sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api-frontend",code!~"4..|5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api-frontend"}[5m]))
- p99 latency (Histogram): histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="inference-runtime"}[5m])) by (le))

Appendix B: FAQ
Q: When should we create a synthetic canary?
A: For any service that impacts customer-facing latency or correctness (e.g., model inference, routing). Start with a minimal prompt set and expand as confidence grows.

Q: How do we handle stateful capacity (KV caches)?
A: Include warmup/rehydration steps in the capacity plan, reserve cross-zone capacity for failover, and test restore under load.
